MeCUAIG (Maple Creek): Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the house and to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) what I think is unfair and unjust treatment imposed upon farmers and small businessmen in respect of income taxation. This applies especially to the part of the country from which I come, where there has been a series of crop failures. For income tax purposes the farmer was unable to carry his losses over from year to year prior to 1944. The income tax law was amended in 1946 in order to remedy this unjust situation, but it went back only to 1944. By this amendment the loss on tihe 1944 operations could be carried into 1945 and subsequent years. But this left huge outstanding losses on operating expense incurred in the years prior to 1944. I should, like to ask the minister: If this principle holds good back to 1944. why not be fair and go the whole way? The principle cannot be changed.
I will give an example in mv own district. In 1936 we had practically a crop failure. We just got seed out of it. In 1937 there was a complete crop failure. There was not one bushel threshed in our district. In 1938 the crop was spotty. In 1939 and 1940 we had the
The Budget-Mr. McCuaig

worst infestation of grasshoppers ever seen in western Canada. In 1941 there was a good crop and in 1942 there was the biggest crop we ever had. This is what happened. Hundreds of farmers were asked to make out income tax returns in the years 1943 and 1944 and to go back as far as 1940. Over the bad years there was a huge accumulation of debts-bank loans, machinery debt, repair bills, store accounts, doctor and hospital bills, back taxes and plenty of other things. The government, instead of giving the farmer a little encouragement, actually ruined the farmer's credit by not allowing him first to pay his debts, which I call his first obligation, to honour the trust and confidence which his fellow men, the Small businessmen in town, had placed in him.
In 1942 there was a quota on wheat. The farmer could sell only so much. The same was true in 1943 and 1944. In 1943 and 1944 income tax inspectors travelled all over the country. The income tax branch and its inspectors completely ignored those past operating losses and allowed only current expenses which came within the income tax exemptions for the one year under review. The farmer was taxed for money which was not his, but which belonged to local businessmen who trusted him, gave him credit and provided him with means to carry on over those trying years. He was taxed to the limit on the income of those years I have mentioned, while he still owed a large amount of money.
Furthermore, there is the matter of the $1,200 exemption. In the years when the farmer had little or no revenue, he could not take advantage of that $1,200 exemption. He went into debt for the necessities of living and cost of operation of the farm. When a better crop year came along, he got the $1,200 exemption for that one year only, but still carried an accumulation of debt from the bad years. He was not permitted to carry forward the exemption of previous years in order to help pay the debts of those years. I want you to see, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer was stuck at both ends of the game, going and coming.
Let me give another instance. The income tax branch ruled that if a car was proved necessary for the carrying on of farming operations, car expense would be allowed. Expenses were allowed but depreciation was not allowed. If depreciation was not an expense, I should like to know what it was. I call it just plain chiselling. I would ask the minister to make a note of that.
The farmer's wife and family put in long hours, before school and after school, working in the garden, milking cows, feeding calves and raising chickens. They were the busiest people on the farm, but they were not allowed one
dollar for their work. When it came to harvesting those things, they were required to give an account of every nickel, for income tax purposes. There was no thought or sympathetic consideration given to the appalling need for better homes, family needs, worn-out machinery and dilapidated buildings or, as was mentioned by an hon. member the other day, a well, which is a most necessary thing, for a farm must have water. After a farmer had spent long years wearing out tanks and wagons in drawing water, and had reached the stage when he had saved up a few dollars and could dig a well, the cost of the digging of this well was not allowed as an operating expense. This was what I call just more plain chiselling.
This is a far cry from the way our big business friends -were treated. Double depreciation was allowed in many cases and, after making huge profits during the war, many government-assisted and built plants were handed back to the big fellows for a mere song. The Crane people were given $400,000. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) called it an incentive subsidy so that they would produce more. There was a large field ahead of this company; consumers were crying for more of their product and were likely to continue to do so for a long time. Why did this private enterprise industry not jump into it with their own capital or borrow money from the banks on their own responsibility, as the farmer has had to do? I think the government was pretty free with the taxpayers' money, money which belonged to the little people whom I am representing. Furthermore, no ceiling was put on the goods this company were making. They got the price they asked and they got subsidies besides; and do not let us forget that they had a complete monopoly on this product.
There is nothing needed more in the world today than food. People can do without bathtubs, but in order to live they must have food. Here we have, as a friendly gesture, $400,000 given to one firm with which to make bathtubs. Many times this amount was chiselled away from the tillers of the soil in income tax and subsidies, which subsidies should have been part of the selling price in the first place, but in my opinion it was called a subsidy so that it could be withdrawn and would not look so bad as would the reducing of prices. The farmers are not asking for an incentive; they are asking only for equity and justice. The most important industry in Canada should be treated on a par with other industries.
While this was going on, the Liberal government was deliberately taking the farmer's wheat and selling it to Canadian consumers

The Budget-Mr. McCuaig
at thirty cents a bushel less than he could get for it on the export market. The stockman got the same kind of deal. A floor price was put underneath his product when it was in the hands of the packer, but no floor price was put under cattle when they were in the hands of the producers. Why was the agriculturist, the humble tiller of the soil, treated in this way? I can only see it as a continuation of the spirit of the feudal lords toward the common man. The concern of our economy is not for the health and welfare of human beings, to provide better homes, better families, better bodies. The concern of our economy is for money, power and control. In the short space of ten years we have seen a lot of material things pass into history. For instance, Mussolini and his gang, Hitler and his gang, Tojo and his gang, all have passed into history. Why? Because there was no place in their philosophy for the teaching of the Man of Galilee: service and humility. Yet it would appear that we have learned nothing. This is the most damning indictment against our so-called democracy today, and I do not think we have the chance of a snowball in the hot place to build a Canadian empire under an economy of this kind. We educate thousands of our children only to have them leave Canada, a land of great potential wealth and beauty. At the present time thousands of our young people are getting married, and they say they are not going to have children; they say they cannot afford to have children.
Oh, oh.

That is quite common, and it is not a laughing matter. It will have a serious reaction on Canada's population in the next twenty years. I have been among these young people, and one hears that said on every hand. The magnificent churches of our cities are only half-filled today; yet the beer parlours are overflowing with men and women.
Oh, oh.

The drink bill is increasing at an alarming rate, and members laugh about it. We are selling millions of bushels of wheat to brewers and distillers, good food which is needed for millions of starving children. Juvenile delinquency, accidents and crimes are increasing, and we have not the accommodation to care properly for fifty per cent of our mentally ill people. A large percentage of our working people are living in homes without modern accommodation, such as bathtubs and toilets. These things are recognized by the public today, as is manifested by delegations, briefs and petitions brought before this government. Just recently a petition was presented in this house bearing the signatures of over a quarter of a million people praying for more humane treatment and care of our old people. The plight of the physically handicapped and war widows was brought to the attention of the government. Public opinion is aroused in Canada today as never before, for the adoption of social Christian principles as propounded by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation: humanity first.
To support this contention, Mr. Speaker, with your kind permission I shall submit some evidence, and from a corner of the house you would hardly expect it. I want to do honour where honour is due, in this case to an hon. member who, I think, is a conscientious and sincere gentleman. I quote from the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), as recorded at page 3179 of Hansard for this session:
We cannot afford any longer to sit still here and take no notice of what is going on in Canada. The danger to our freedom is greater from within Canada than from without.
What is Canada's answer to all this? First, we should put our own place in order, overhaul the British North America Act and revise our parliamentary system and the other systems I have named. We should adopt some system of Christian socialism for the workers of this country, the white-collar employees, the artisans and the farmers. A system of Christian socialism-
What is that?

I will give the hon. member a copy of the C.C.F. national manifesto. Further on, the hon. member had this to say:
In the debate on constitutional reform on February 17, 1937, I referred to how the provincial legislatures were created, and I had a word to say in relation to industrial employment, contrasting the precepts of Christianity with the way in which our industrial workers are used. Personality counts as nothing; the dollar is all supreme. Modern life is machine life, soulless, a life of standardization, a high speed production, a highly efficient organization for the making of profits. Dividends are the chief objective; to get dividends, human beings are sacrificed. Wages were often below the level of mere subsistence, so that people were forced into other ways of life to eke out a precarious livelihood. I spoke of the long hours of work exacted, but reforms have been brought aibout in that. Senior employees, after long years of faithful service, were in many cases cast out without a retiring allowance to make room for younger people. I said that the law of Christ, that we should bear one another's burdens, was not being carried out.
Apparently the hon. member for Broadview knows the monopolistic bible. Two thousand years ago, Mr. Speaker, it was said, "Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" and "A contrite heart and humble spirit should lead them." I wish the hon. member for Broadview every success and the best of luck in his evangelistic work in the Tory camp.
The Budget-Mr. A. L. Smith

The espionage trials and other activities have led to a virtual campaign against communism and a spirit of hate against the U.S.S.R., not only in Canada but in the United States. Witch hunting and building capitalist bridgeheads around our democracies is the order of the day. The purpose of this is to prevent the communist ideology and philosopny from spreading farther into the western world.
As a practical man and a solid Canadian, who got his education in the hard school of trial and error, in practical application and results, I would say that we are starting at the wrong end and using an entirely wrong method to remedy this most dangerous situation between neighbours. The U.S.S.R. philosophy and their way of life is their own business, in their own country, and, if it is attractive to our people, we shall not stop it here by force, or government-sponsored subversive action. We can do it only by showing the world that we have something better-not in flowery words, but in the manner of practical application, in the utilization and distribution of all our great resources in the interests of all our people in Canada. This was the purpose of creation, and it is for the interests of mankind.
Let us put man on the pedestal, and show all the world that we glorify God's greatest handiwork-man in the image of his Maker. And let us do some straight thinking abouf this. If we do so we need not be afraid of any ism in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have not usurped much of your time during this session, and even though I push prorogation half an hour farther toward Christmas, I propose to make a few remarks at this time. I assure you that in dealing with the budget I shall endeavour neither to thresh old straw nor to advance any new economic ideology.
Having been in the house now for my third session of parliament, I thought I might usefully make some remarks concerning my observations of what we have been doing. I begin by complimenting the House of Commons. under your able direction, sir, upon the splendid tone generally maintained in our debates. I am not suggesting that in this respect we are all free from guilt. A week or so ago I saw my own name in the paper in connection with a short debate in which I took part in an exchange with one of the ministers. I assure you, sir, that I did not read with pride what I said on that occasion. I sincerely trust my adversary at that time would hold the same view concerning what he said.
Those were little things. But it seems to me the absolute low in political public discussion was reached here the other night in the maiden speech of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Hartt). Speeches of that kind are not going to do us any good. However, you, sir, and hon. members have the satisfaction of knowing that if there is any change it must be for the better; it cannot be any lower than the bottom of the barrel.
I turn now to some matters concerning which I think there might be some improvement. I appreciate Your Honour's difficulty in dealing with questions asked when the orders of the day are called. I am conscious, too, of the difficulty you must have in making spot decisions as to a question's urgency or relevancy. It seems to me that we would do well to adopt the practice in the British House of Commons whereby, so many times each week, a definite time is set aside when questions may be asked of the government, and when there is no particular matter of urgency to be decided.
I must, however, offer some little criticism of the two ministers who unfortunately are not at the moment in their seats. I refer to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I am sure no one would suggest for one moment that hon. members on this side ask any questions in which there could be political implications.
Oh, oh.

I should think that would be generally assumed by the house. I would rate those two ministers by stating that the Minister of Labour wins all championships, not only through his failure to answer questions he is asked, but also for including politics in every reply he makes. The Minister of Finance is not a good second; indeed he is well down the list. I would not care to classify the rest of the field. It seems to me, however, that questions are not meant for that purpose. And, lest there be any doubt about the matter let me say that I was speaking ironically, because I know it does come from both sides of the house.
Having said that, I turn to a matter which has arisen in outstanding form during this session. I refer to the procedure of mixing legislative matters in one bill. We had, of course, the omnibus bill, and I appreciate it is not intended that the practice set up in that bill shall be followed. Perhaps it represented an unusual occasion. But, more important-and there was no reason for this -we had in one piece of legislation the

The Budget-Mr. A. L. Smith
coupling of immigration with Chinese exclusion. There is nothing mutual about those subjects, and it seems to me that they should not have been placed in one bill.
Indeed the situation is like it would be if Your Honour were to ask me out to dinner- and may I add that that is not a hint-and you placed before me some caviar. I then tell you that I do not like caviar, as a result of which you say to me, "You eat the whole dinner, including the printer's name on the menu, or you eat nothing at all." That is exactly the position in which we are placed when the government ties together in one piece of legislation subjects which should be the subject matter of two or three bills, or whatever number the subjects would justify.
My next complaint is not against the government, but it is one for which, it seems to me, there should be a remedy. I refer to the utter lack of trained people in this building who could be of assistance to private members who are honestly trying to find out something about a subject in which they may be interested. I go all the way with what was said last year by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), because private members on the government side and also on this side may find ourselves interested in a subject which would be dealt with in a department of one of the ministers. We may think that the government is wrong, and that an error in judgment is being made, and may feel that another course should be adopted.
What do we find? We find we must do all our own digging. This is in no sense a criticism of the few splendid people we have in the library. We just have not the kind of people I think we should have, and in my view it would be good for parliament and for the country if ministers were attacked a little more often.
One may make up his mind that a piece of legislation is totally bad, or that some of it is bad. I am not suggesting for one moment that it is intentionally that way. I refer to an honest difference of opinion. He comes into the House of Commons with what little assistance he can find and attacks the piece of legislation. The moccasin telegraph immediately gets working to the official gallery, and, in ten minutes or so, three, four, five, ten or fifty-take whatever number you want- people begin to work to show that you are wrong even though they know you are right. In other words, they attempt to find little reasons here and there to show that the fellow on the opposite side is wrong, even 83166-214
though they know he is right. It seems to me that that is carried a very long distance.
Let us assume that I ask a question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I do not see him here and I am getting lonesome-oh, yes, I have found him now. Let us assume that I ask the Minister of National Defence what has happened to a certain thousand men in some camp in some remote spot in this country. Immediately the boys go to work and the first answer I get is that there is no camp with one thousand men. Sergeant Cook has ulcers of the stomach and is off strength for the moment, so the answer is given that I am just completely wrong.
Then he will carry on, "I will tell you how completely wrong you are because, by order in council 947,777, which I now table, it shows that the whole command was disbanded and there is nobody there at all." He will continue, "That order in council is 947,777A, because the treasury branch did not want to pass 947,778." I am beaten before I start, simply because I am unable to find any means in this building whereby I can gather the facts I need. It is easy to say to a private member, "Why do you not go and dig?" This is the ordinary life of a member of parliament in Ottawa as I have found it. I am not an early riser but I try to get here by ten o'clock.
Good.

I am happy the hon. member thinks it is good. At eleven o'clock you have'committees to attend; you have your lunch; you sit from three to six and from eight to eleven; in the meantime you take care of your correspondence and the errands you have to run and that sort of thing. Most of us live here in an atmosphere which is not good-I am referring to the air- for at least twelve hours a day. It just is not possible for anyone, unless he maintains a clipping service out of his own pocket, unless he pays research people himself, to have a sufficient and exhaustive knowledge of any subject in which he is interested. I mention these things in the ordinary life which we live.
In addition to that, we have all the reports of the committees. For example, we want to go home and be able to know something of what the veterans committee-it is not sitting this year

or the Indian committee or some other committee has been doing. We all try to keep up as well as we can with what has been accomplished. We should be able to go to someone and say, "Let me have a summary of what has taken place there." It is true that

The Budget-Mr. A. L. Smith

we have secretaries, but I doubt very much if many hon. members have secretaries who are capable of doing that. I am happy to say that I have an excellent secretary, but as yet I have not asked her to go through that business.
I turn now to a matter which interests the country greatly, the leadership of the Liberal party. I should like to give some excellent advice, because I know there are many people interested in knowing just where the mantle will fall. I have been watching some of the aspirants very carefully across the floor for some time, and I say to them that they should get out more into the country. As far as the people in the area in which I live are concerned, they could have two heads because they really do not know them. It may be that they prefer the anonymity-perhaps that is the wrong word-it may be that they prefer not to be seen, but I think they are all gentlemen of not undistinguished countenances and certainly we should like to see more of them in the part of the country in which I live. My last thought is 'that they should adopt the method employed a long time ago and simply cast lots for the mantle and settle the thing quickly in a friendly fashion.
I turn now to the budget. Every hon. member has complimented the Minister of Finance. I intend to do likewise, but only in one particular. I am always interested in forensic efforts whenever I find them, and I think one of the finest exhibitions I have ever seen was when the Minister of Finance used some words that will long remain in my mind. He stood up to his not inconsiderable height; his voice was resonant and ringing, and he gave an example of the greatest courage ever exhibited by a public man when he looked across here and with flashing eye and ringing tones said, "This is a real surplus." I compliment him upon that kind of performance. It was an oratorical effort which I think I shall long remember.
If this is a real surplus, then the minister can push water up hill with a sieve. He reversed all the ordinary laws of accountancy. If he still uses the method that he used here I am quite sure that he could upset Newton's law of gravity, and it would take most of us until tomorrow to find out that perhaps he was wrong.
I mention one other thing, a thing which, of course, is not political. I heard on the radio last night that a bridge was to be built between Halifax and Dartmouth, and I heard something about certain marsh lands in Nova Scotia. May I say that anything I say at the moment about the maritimes I want to preface with the statement that is usually found in books: Any reference to any person living

or dead is purely coincidental. Taking my mind back through history, I remember that Lief Ericson discovered Nova Scotia some five or six hundred years ago. I was unable to find in the library any of Lief's memoirs, but I am sure that at that time he had something to say about the marsh lands of Nova Scotia. You will remember that Longfellow wrote a poem about the Acadians; this is the forest primeval, the murmuring pines and the hemlocks, and so on. That was his great poem, "Evangeline." I am sure the only reason Longfellow did not write about the marsh lands was that he died before he could really get anything ready on the marsh lands.
I have been reading Hansard for a considerable number of years and I can assure you, sir, that I have read of these marsh lands being discussed at almost every session of parliament for a great many years. I want you to believe me when I say I am sure that this is purely coincidental and has nothing to do with a certain by-election to be held in Halifax a month or so from now.
I shall mention only two things in connection with the budget. I mention, first, one little thing, and I do so only because I do not think I have received as many communications about any other subject as I have about this little matter of the tax on soft drinks. These letters come from Y.M.C.A.'s, church organizations and others. I have no doubt the drive was organized, but they all seem to feel keenly about this tax, and I think it it not yet too late to have this little bit of tax taken off.
I want to say a word about something which is not in the budget and which, I think, is not in the estimates of the Department of National Health, and I do so because, next to the soft drink matter, I am quite sure that my correspondence with respect to the disease of arthritis has been heavier than on any other subject. If I suggest to you. sir, that I speak feelingly on this subject I hope you will not think I am trying to make a pun; nevertheless it would go both ways.
When we hear, as we did last year from the then minister of health, that 600,000 of our population of 12,000.000 are suffering from this crippling disease, it does seem to me that no time should be wasted to find out, by way of research, why this thing is and, for those who already have the disease, what the cure may be. I realize that members in opposition are constantly suggesting to a government that it should go and spend money here and there. We want the government to do something in the west, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) so well put it and as so many others have put it. We want this and the

The Budget-Mr. A. L. Smith
other fellows want that and, I suppose, if one took a pencil and added up all these proposed expenditures they might reach a staggering sum beyond the capability perhaps of any government to provide. So that it comes down to this: it becomes a matter of judgment for the government itself as to how the money we have can best be spent. Mr. Speaker, I recommend this expenditure on the cause and cure of arthritis, not only to relieve suffering-and it is intense in many cases and there are many sufferers-but because it has a bearing on our economic life, so much so that one could almost call this expenditure a self-liquidating project. The blow it strikes at our economic life through making 600.000 of our people unable to work is an argument on the economic side which might perhaps assist the minister in dealing with the treasury board.
I come now to discuss something of a serious nature, namely the wheat board. I have some figures. I am not asking permission to put them on Hansard by just filing a piece of paper, because I want to read them to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). But first I want to say this. There has been no meeting of the agricultural committee of this house, I think since 1942. At no time in the history of the wheat board since 1936 have the audited accounts of that board ever been placed on the table of the House of Commons. I do not want to be misunderstood. I realize that, by statute and in fact, statements have been filed by the board itself, but no audited statements have ever been filed as such and were never filed before any public body in Canada until a few weeks ago when they were tabled in a senate committee. It is unfortunate that at that committee there was no reporter, so that only one copy of the statement was available. I did get a quick glance at it and, with assistance, extracted from it some figures which I should like to give to the house.

Mr. Speaker, when the house was good enough to give me three or four minutes at the dinner recess I assured you I intended to deal with only one other subject. I intend to live up to what I then said, but I must make this admission. I have listened with some care to the speeches made in this the greatest of all deliberative bodies in the Dominion of Canada, and I have noticed that, whoever speaks, whether it be on a bridge over a creek in his back yard or on 83166-214J
baby bonuses or on international affairs, we have all become accustomed to the statement that it is the greatest problem facing the Canadian people at this particular time. Perhaps it is in our own bailiwick, but I do not pretend for a moment that what I am about to say ranks in that class at all.
As I indicated then, I intend for the first time in my life-I mean my life in this House of Commons-to use some figures, and these figures concern the wheat board of this country. And lest my hon. and very close and old friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) has any doubt about them, I can only say to him that I do not see any of his cohorts upstairs at the moment. I give him these figures on my responsibility as a member of parliament, and I say that as to their approximate correctness. By approximate correctness, I mean that there will be no deviation of over one per cent, and in any event it will be a very small figure.
This wheat board of ours cost, in 1939, in administrative and overhead expenses, S677.342; in 1942. $842,149; in 1945. $1,592,543. ATou will remember that this is all handling the same crop. I will admit they did take up some minor things like rape seed and a few incidentals which do not very much restrict or enlarge the picture. I may say to you, sir, that the increase there is 134 per cent between 1939 and 1915, and between 1942 and 1945 it is still 89 per cent.
I turn to some individual items and, first, I deal with the question of salaries. Before I go farther, may I assure everyone here that I am not at all presuming, or suggesting from these figures, any dishonesty or anything even savouring of that on the part of those who operate the wheat board. When I have given 3'ou these figures I intend to try to draw an inference which I think is quite fair and which has been consistent with the attitude taken by those of us who are in this parliament. I have extracted a number of items as follows:

I will get rid of all my figures and then I shall have some comment to make upon them. In the period, from 1936, when it was instituted, to 1945, the end of the crop year of 1944, this board lost in its operations $112 million. I wish to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and the house, how that was paid. They took a credit of S24,S(X),000 from their predecessor. They have obtained from the dominion treasury $87,450,000, and that is divided into two amounts. On July 31, 1945, they received 867,469,000, and at that time there was charged up and still to be drawn, $19,9SO,000. So you see how the loss has been made up.
One other item I intend to call to your attention and it is this. The balance sheet of July 31, 1945, shows that they have set up

and I quote exactly: "provision for expenses of issuing final payments", presumably referring to payment out of a residue of $10,377,597, or, in other words, ten per cent of the total, for issuing the final cheques with respect to the balances outstanding on participation certificates to farmers for that year. I said, sir, that I had no intention of charging against the wheat board anything savouring of dishonesty, or anything of that kind. But what I do say is that we in this party

endeavoured to have this matter referred to a committee where there might be an examination of the operation of this board, but we were refused that by the government. May I also say that both the groups to my left, if my memory serves me correctly, voted with the government, although I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) voted with us on that occasion. Remembering that they were handling the wheat crop of western Canada-that'is not exactly all; there were other little duties added-I put this to you, sir, with great respect, that we have never had any explanation. Can you imagine that? We had great difficulty with the Department of Trade and Commerce. It took us at least six weeks in this house to find out what balance they had on their hands for the 1945 crop. But can you imagine it?-in salaries, there was a 266 per cent increase; in rentals, 117 per cent; postage and excise, 1,403 per cent; audit fees, 286 per cent; tabulating equipment-and that is a big word-223 per cent; travel, 515 per cent. All that without any explanation whatever having been given to this House of Commons!
I base my criticism on two grounds. I think even the most rabid-thinking person who sits opposite to me or to my left will agree that I am at least fair in this. My argument is twofold. The first is that if ever accounts required examination by the House of Commons, those accounts of the wheat board, of which I have given you instances, require examination. Perhaps I should have given the over-all figure. It is this. In 1939. total administration and overhead amounted to $677,342; in 1942, 1842,149; in 1945, $1,592,543, or an increase, over-all, of 134 per cent in 1945 and 89 per cent in 1942. As I say, my criticism is twofold. I say that is something which should have had examination by the standing committee on agriculture. Just to mention this increase in astronomical figures is to say enough, it seems to me, almost to force on the mind of any fair-minded person that they are at least worthy of examination.
My second criticism is this. Here we are paying in one year to a firm of auditors, whose name escapes me at the moment, although I think Brown is the first name in the firm-
Brown, Brown and Brown.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member over there is colour blind.

Frankly, I know I am getting a little bit deaf, but I do not like these whispering campaigns. The point I make is that this is one place at least, having regard to all our crown companies,

The Budget-Mr. A. L. Smith
where this audit should be in the hands of Mr. Sellar, auditor general of the Dominion of Canada. I have not actually seen the auditor's certificate, but I assume it is that usually meaningless thing which is attached to every audit-where they say, we have seen this and. we have seen that; the papers we asked for have been forthcoming, and so on- which, through sad experience in the courts, they have been driven to do and which, as we all now know, means nothing. But if the auditor general of the Dominion of Canada had these figures which I have now read, does anyone think he would not have had some comment to make with respect to them? I would ask the house to remember that we are continuing this wheat, board now at least to the end 'of the British wheat agreement. The people over here at the moment want to continue it forever. I am quite sure they will change their minds about that as circumstances develop. But this is not a business where you need research people, or where you need great technical experts. It is just a bunch of people buying selling wheat, and that has been going on since the world began. Why this particular government company or crown company-call it what you like-is not under the auditor general and is not under the civil service is something that I at least-and it may be my fault-am completely incapable of understanding. Nor in the discussion on the Wheat Board Act did we receive any explanation from either the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who collaborated so closely, as the house will remember, in answering some of the embarrassing questions which were then asked. We have not yet heard one reason given why that should not be so. I imagine it is a continuous audit. You could not pay $58,000, I am sure, unless it were a continuous audit. I have no doubt there are a bunch of bright boys over there who are learning chartered accountancy, and they were counting cheques and counting dollars and using this $62,569 of tabulating equipment rather well. I imagine they are not one-finger fellows. They can probably play the equipment as a man or woman plays a piano. But when we pay $58,000 a year, sir, for an. audit, and all we get is just what I have told you, then it seems to me that Mr. Watson Sellar should be called in.
I close, sir, by repeating that I am not making any sign of a charge of dishonesty against anybody. But I say that this business has now cost the taxpayer $100 million odd, aside from what it has cost the farmer. This
board made so much money, but their total loss over that area I have given is $100 million odd. What we are doing here is launching into something the end of which we know not.
Let us take two other institutions which are both government-owned and operated. Let us take. Trans-Canada Air Lines and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We all remember the history of the Canadian National Railways, and we all know they have been burrowing into the treasury of this country all these years. Now T.C.A. has started. Last year the C.B.C. lost $409,000, and this year will lose $500,000. There is only one place that money can come from. What we are doing, generally speaking, by these crown companies, these government operated, companies, is just starting another snowball which the taxpayers of this country, through their dollars, will have to provide the energy and strength to push back up the hill whence it came.

Mr. Speaker, over the week-end I had the occasion to discuss at length with a group of my constituents who belong to the working class, the different measures now before the house and I was asked to express my opinion on the budget. I answered that I would do so in the very near future and so, with your permission and relying on the indulgence of hon. members, the voice of Shefford will once more be heard in this chamber.
On September 10, 1939, Canada declared, war on Germany and on May 8, 1945, the united nations achieved final victory over their enemies. In just about a quarter of a century, our country had been through a second great war which had lasted six long years.
According to an old saying which I heard not so long ago, when your neighbour's house is on fire you must lend a helpful hand, if you want to protect your own buildings. Once the fire is extinguished, the victims are left to themselves to assess the damage and one often forgets all about his own efforts, although they may eventually have serious consequences.
I must say that on April 29 of this year, while listening to the financial resolutions submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), I was reminded of this saying with the only difference that instead of a fire it was a war. Having lent a helpful hand to our allies, we know what will be the effect of that help on our financial position. Worrying serves no purpose; the consequences of our gesture will long be felt, but it is to be hoped that those whom we have helped will do likewise unto us, should we ever need their assistance.
The Budget-Mr. Boivin

Like hon. members who have spoken before me, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to offer my most sincere congratulations to the Minister of Finance for the splendid way in which he presented his first budget. One can readily see that upon taking charge of his new department, he did everything he could to reduce considerably wartime expenses and I sincerely hope that he will continue to do so during the present fiscal year, in order to help the Canadian people who sorely need further tax reductions at the present time.
The members of this house were pleased to hear the Minister of Finance render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's when he paid the following tribute to his predecessor:
Behind us are the huge and difficult budgets of the war years-high water marks of achievement set by a minister of finance whose name will long be remembered and honoured by his fellow Canadians.
All hon. members will acclaim that statement and they understand that the present Minister of Justice had a hard and thankless task during the war, as Minister of Finance. In addition to providing a sound financial administration he prevented inflation.
You will agree, Mr. Speaker, that inflation threatened all countries of the world, save Canada, thanks to his wisdom and perspicacity, thanks also to the sagacity and foresight of those whom he selected for the task of protecting the stability of our currency.
There have been many shortages, it is true, owing to the many difficulties encountered by manufacturers and because a great number of them found it impossible to obtain raw materials. But through the department which came under his wing, the wartime prices and trade board, prices were held in constant check. In this way, Canadians saved millions and millions of dollars. I admit readily that he directed his department in a masterly fashion with the wise help of the Prime Minister, who has been leading our fair party for the past 27 years and has proved to the world that Canada could grow as well under a sound administration in times of stress as in years of prosperity.
On behalf of French-speaking members, may I congratulate most sincerely our Englishspeaking colleagues upon their successful efforts in learning our language. You have been listening, these last few days, to the hon. members for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). To the latter, who has experienced great difficulty in learning French, I extend my, congratulations and those of my colleagues. The hon. member for Calgary West should try to imitate his col-

leagues instead of passing remarks. Thereby he wrould help his own people and contribute to a greater extent to the unity of Canada.
As I have already stated in this house, I belonged to the working class until June 11, 1945. Therefore, paragraphs 3 and 4 of the budget speech aroused my interest. For this reason I should like to refer to it and to call the attention of the minister of finance to certain statements, in order to assist the workingman and the small wage-earner. The minister said:
Our available manpower is almost fully employed.
It is true that there is no scarcity of manpower, but even with the lifting of wage controls and the granting of small wage increases, the low wage-earner is still experiencing financial difficulties.
For instance, let us take the case of a labourer who, in 1940, was receiving $18 per week. He was then paying 25 cents for two pounds of steak, $20 for a suit of clothes, $4 for a pair of shoes, $2 for a hat and proportionate prices for other items. Now let us suppose that in recognition of his devotion to duty and his hard work, his employer has given him an increase of $16 a week-if so he is more fortunate than most of his fellow workers-and he is now receiving $34 per week. However, he must now pay 50 cents per pound for steak-and not of the best quality at that- $60 to $65 for a suit-more in many cases- S10 for shoes and higher prices for all other items. In order to bear out those statements, I got in touch with a dealer in men's furnishings of Granby who told me that prices of goods have increased generally by 20 per cent from 1940 to 1946 and in some eases by 60 per cent since the lifting of controls. Generally the quality is much lower.
It must be admitted that wages have not gone up at the same rate as the cost of living. I trust a solution may be found and I even wonder if decontrol has not been too hasty.
Mr. Speaker, if I remember rightly, at the time of the last budget I requested exemptions of $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons. Now, about personal income tax, in going over the new schedule, I recalled the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley's statement to the effect that:
The income tax is the fairest and best tax on which to rely for the hulk of our revenue. More than any other, it takes ability to pay properly into account and this applies as well in the lower brackets as in the higher.
I have often given thought to those words and while we have been told that last year's exemptions of $750 and $1,500 were high enough to relieve more than 50 per cent of

The Budget-Mr. Boivin
Canadian wage-earners from all income tax,
I feel it was not properly taken into account. For instance let us go into the financial situation of a single man earning $100 a month, or $1,200 a year.
As a first item, his room rent is now $6 a week, or $312 a year. His meals, at a minimum of 50 cents, cost him $1.50 a day, $10.50 a week or $546 a year. That is item No. 2. Let us allow him, say, $2.50 weekly for cigarettes and pocket money and we have a third item of $130 a year. Now allow the same taxpayer $60 for a single suit of clothes during the year, $50 for an overcoat, $5 for a hat, $10 for a pair of shoes, a minimum of $25 for handkerchiefs, socks, shirts, ties and underwear and $50 for working clothes. Allowing only a minimum in each case, item No. 4 amounts to $200 a year. Under item No. 5, we have medical treatment for an amount of at least $50. This does not take into account any time lost nor casual expenses and yet it provides only a bare existence and not by any means a decent standard of living.
But I was forgetting, Mr. Speaker, that the same individual is subject to income tax. Looking at the table given by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, I find that on an income of $11200 a year he must pay by cheque to the order of the Receiver General of Canada, the sum of $61 representing item No. 6. If we add up those several amounts, we get a total of $1,299, which means a deficit of $99.
Now let us take as an example, the married man with two dependent children and a salary of $2,000 a year. There we have:
Minimum rent, $30 a month, $360 a year.
Electricity, $4.50 a month, $54 a year.
Recreation for the family, $4 a week, $208 a year.
Clothing, for himself, $200 per annum.
Clothing, for his wife, $100 per annum.
Clothing, for his children, $150 per annum.
Food, $3 a day, minimum $1,095 per annum.
Medical expenses, $100 per annum.
Life insurance, householder, ignoring the rest of the family, $84 per annum.
Fire insurance, $8 per annum.
Income tax, $36 per annum.
Omitting household and miscellaneous expenditures, we have a total of $2,395 per annum.
To be generous, let us deduct family allowances of $7 and $8 a month, or $15 a month, $180 per annum.
The total becomes $2,215, representing a deficit of $215.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this married man earning $2,000, even after receiving family allowances worth $180, still shows a deficit of $215 and runs into debt.
When his children are a little older, he will find some excuse, in spite of compulsory education, to keep them out of school so that they may help him, not to clear himself from debt, but to balance his budget.
From the example which I have submitted today, it will be realized, I trust, that expenses must be further reduced and that the worker must be granted enough of an exemption to meet his obligations, for it must not be forgotten that if he is financially successful the country benefits by it.
Note that the above-mentioned tables are based on $1,200 and $2,000 exemptions. How would the figures compare if I had compiled this information according to the $750 and $1,500 exemptions in effect in 1946?
I was not in the least surprised to read in the newspapers that on March 31, 1946, 328,288 Canadians had not yet paid their income tax. I fear that, under present conditions, the number will increase. For that reason, I entirely agree with what the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) said in this house on May 12 last, about income tax and the payment of interest by taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, although I have proven that, in my opinion, the present exemption is too low, I admit that this budget is very interesting. I had looked forward to an increase in exemptions but the government decided instead to decrease the income tax 29 per cent on the average. The reduction is as high as 54 per cent in the case of those in the lower income brackets and thus, it will benefit the working class.
I have carefully noted what the minister said on April 29 last. I quote:
Some increases in inventories are occurring out apparently not on a large scale, presumably oecause the pressure of demand in most cases is so excessive that neither producers nor dealers can keep ahead of it.
Later on, he said:
. . . most of our imports have had to come from the United States.
In that connection I must say that at the present time commercial travellers are selling large quantities of American goods to our stores at a much higher price; such a condition is disadvantageous to the Canadian people who will have to pay more for the goods, but it is also unfavourable to our own industry which will find the market overstocked when it is in a position to produce at full capacity.
The Budget-Mr. Boivin

Speaking of the working class, the Minister of Finance mentioned dwellings and said there was still an acute shortage in spite of all the efforts to alleviate it.
There is no room for doubt in my mind, after listening on January 7 to the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) to the effect that despite shortages of materials, 59,846 housing units had been built in 1946 and that construction of 80,000 units was contemplated in 1947.
I am very anxious to know the cost of houses which have been built with a great deal of difficulty without the help of a government subsidiary. I know very well that in 1946 nobody could obtain nails anywhere except on the great market which became popular with many people and which is still called the black market. Gyproc could be had on the same market, for a small consideration. To secure any plumbing material, one had to oil somebody's palm, even when oil was scarce.
On July 11, 1946, page 3342 of Hansard, I dealt with a few points in connection with building. I now wish to add that construction of theatres, garages, restaurants, summer cottages, and all buildings detrimental to the providing of materials required for private homes should be suspended for a certain period of time.
Allow me to quote from an article published in La Voix de I'Est, Granby's daily neswaper, on February 21, 1947 under the heading "Significant Figures on the Need of Houses for Workers". This report told of a survey launched in 25 urban centres by a workers' league. It showed that only 5-9 per cent of the workers owned their homes in my province.
Those statistics also reveal overcrowding; there are an average of 6-76 persons per housing unit whereas each unit contains only 4-67 rooms. In 60-4 homes there is no dining room, and in 34-6 there is no living room. In 12-4 per cent of cases, people sleep in the kitchen; in 23-8 per cent in the dining room and in 41-4 per cent in the living room. This survey shows that steps should be taken to remedy the situation.
The minister has referred in the budget speech to the high level of our production and income, owing to a large extent to our export trade. It is true that Canada exports more goods than she consumes and that exports are necessary. The minister insisted on the fact that the export credit programme was essentially a transitional measure.
He also made a statement which the people of Canada had been expecting for a long time when he added that the government did

not contemplate a continuing, large-scale programme of government lending to finance our exports to other countries.
It is true that we have done our full share to help our allies when they were in danger, and I note with pleasure, from the speech of the minister, that we are returning to a business basis and I trust that notwithstanding the increased prices we shall not be called upon to make further extended loans to England or to any other country, which would be detrimental to our own interests.
May I now broach another topic of keen interest to my own constituents, agriculture, which, in so far as it applies to other parts of Canada, takes up a large share of the debates in this house. There has been a call for increased production through proper use of abundant farm machinery and improved methods of cultivation, undoubtedly with a view to boost our foreign markets. It should be noted, however, that our export policy is such as to make it impossible for a great many of our farmers to keep producing at the increased rate they have been doing, at the wise suggestion of experts. Box cars have all been requisitioned for the transport of goods, for the shipment of grain for overseas so that what little grain is shipped to eastern Canada is often sold milled and sacked, at consequently higher prices though of lower quality, while slow deliveries often puts farmers in a difficult position. I hope we may look forward to improvement in this respect and that the present handicaps to the Quebec farmers will be removed with the help of the departments concerned.
In closing, I should like to extend my deepest congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance for setting the course of his financial policy for the general purpose of avoiding inflation as far as practicable and thus assuring Canada of a farm and industrial production that will make ours one of the world's least unfortunate if not most prosperous of nations.

Mr. Speaker, the speech of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) surely created a great impression at the time it was made. However, there is a but. The following analysis of it in this house and outside is a sure indication that the proposed budget does not at all meet the expectations of the average taxpayer, nor his wishes.
Had the minister considered the numerous representations submitted to us in the last months, he surely would have realized, for one thing, that, in connection with the income tax, the small taxpayer expected an increase in the exemption to at least $2,500 for married

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
men and SI ,500 for single persons. It has already been amply proved that the $1,500 exemption granted the married man is absolutely inadequate and that the present rates of taxation applying to incomes of family men, assume a character that is detrimental to families and even anti-social. However, there is another very serious disadvantage arising from the deduction at the source; I do not mean to criticize the system itself, for I consider it commendable. I claim that were we to lighten the burden of taxation for those in the lower income brackets, we would, at the same time, remove, for thousands of taxpayers, the inconveniences resulting from the administration of this system.
We all know that, at the present time, the employer has to deduct part of his employee's salary, on the assumption that his total income will be based on the wages paid to him. If the job is temporary or intermittent, as is often the case, the wage-earner may subsequently be unemployed for a certain period, or he may have to be satisfied with a lower salary, so that, at the end of the year, when everything is reckoned, he would find out that his total income for the twelve months does not reach the amount of the exemption he is entitled to. Then he will have to get busy and write the proper authorities to claim the amount deducted from his salary and it will be many months, sometimes a year, before he recovers those deductions.
A very large proportion of wage-earners have the tax deducted at the source and are in the position I have outlined; hence, by raising the exemptions, we would avoid the inconvenience and trouble incidental to deductions at the source for thousands of taxpayers, while at the same time, making a social contribution.
If the government must, on the one hand, take the required means to collect needed revenue, it should, on the other hand, try to spare its citizens troublesome practices that are hardly profitable but prompt those upon whom they are inflicted to criticize and protest. often with full justification.
There is no doubt that it has cost the government a great deal to collect these insignificant sums deducted at the source, and it is obvious that the checking required when claims are submitted and the mailing of refunds have put the treasury to considerable expense.
How often have we not heard complaints from dissatisfied workers who, after a few months employment, find that the few dollars so essential to them and their families are deducted from their pay. They know that they can claim a refund, but they are also
fully aware that it will not be forthcoming for many a month. Then, they voice their criticism, grumble against the state and society and claim that they are unfairly treated: as a result, they become fertile soil for the development of subversive ideas.
I honestly believe that the government should have increased the non-taxable portion of income and, in order to maintain its returns at the same level, it should have lowered the exemption granted taxpayers in the upper brackets.
Other taxes should also have been eliminated. I refer to those which are generally known as nuisance taxes. The revenue which they provide could easily be derived from other sources and 'their repeal would bring the people a measure of comfort far outweighing the receipts accruing from said taxes.
In wartime, the people willingly submitted to these taxes because they were ready to make all sorts of sacrifice, but now that the war has been over for two years, they are entitled to some slight relief. Moreover, the circumstances under which these taxes were introduced must not be forgotten. Not only was it necessary to fill the treasury coffers with the funds required for the pursuit of our war effort, but the idea was to curtail, as far as possible, the demad for the goods thus taxed. Due to wartime needs, it became imperative to apply strict restrictions on the consumption of all goods, save those of an essential nature.
Although the purchasing power was very high, the government could more easily convince the people that they should make use of that power to purchase war savings certificates and war bonds; today, however, circumstances are entirely different. The reasons which motivated that kind of taxes no longer exist and the government should help the Canadian people to return as quickly as possible to a normal life and enable consumers to obtain more easily the goods of which they were partially or totally deprived during the war.
This debate on the budget gives us the best opportunity of stating and submitting to the government, and to the population as a whole, the needs and representations of our fellow-citizens.
I take this opportunity to make a few remarks on Canada's internal policy and also to indicate my constituents' views on our external policy.

May I ask the hon. member a question before he deals with our external policy? Will he vote for or against the budget?
334S
The Budget-Mr. Donon

The hon. member will no
doubt see for himself when I have finished my speech.
I am not so sure about that.

As far as internal policy is concerned, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the question of foremost interest to the Canadian taxpayers is the matter of dominion-provincial relations. Judging from the speeches made during this debate, I would say that that question was the subject of a great many of them. I do not hesitate to say that I was particularly interested in the speech made yesterday afternoon by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault). The hon. member for Bonaventure who, on that occasion, supported centralization of power-and I congratulate him upon his courage-employed two arguments. First, he contends that the dominion government should have greater power in the fields of direct and indirect taxes, in order to prevent the depression which we may have to face two or three years hence. He summed up his thought in one sentence, which I find on page 3310 of Hansard. Here is what he said: -in making such offers to the provinces, the dominion government is seeking to avoid the next depression, which would be the fifteenth.
The hon. member for Bonaventure spoke to us about the first fourteen depressions the world has known during the past hundred and fifty years. He submitted, as I have shown by quoting his own words, that in order to prevent the next depression, the central government should be granted extended powers.
I well remember the last depression, Mr. Speaker. The others occurred before my tim7, and I did not witness them. I recall, however, that in 1929 and during the following years, many countries experienced a depression as severe as that which bore down on Canada and perhaps more so. Yet they did not have to contend with provincial legislatures. Take England, for instance. Obviously England did not have to cooperate with provincial governments. France was ruled by one central government. Belgium, Holland and many other countries where there existed no provincial governments were hit by the depression as severely as Canada and suffered even more bitterly.
Obviously it is very easy to make a statement, but arguments are needed to support such a stand. Personally, I know that during the twenty-seven years that I have been a practising lawyer, had I asserted, whenever I took up a case in court : "Your Honour, my client is right", that would not have been

sufficient for me to win my case. Such a statement must be based on facts which can support it. In many instances, as I have just shown, many countries that had but a central government, were unable to prevent depressions; that is clear and obvious.
In one European country, the depression was less severe than in others. Indeed, I remember that in 1933, when Hitler came to power in Germany7 and began to prepare his country7 for the terrible and devastating war from which the world has just emerged, the depression was much less acute there than elsewhere; note, however, the kind of economic and political system that country submitted to during the years which were the forerunners of the dreadful catastrophe. Every-one knows that Hitler enslaved his people and shot his political opponents. If that is the type of economic and political system the hon. member advocates in order to prevent depressions, I will have none of it and much prefer democratic systems like our own, even though that may mean putting up with the drawbacks of depressions -which, nevertheless, could easily be avoided if we took the proper means.
The second argument which the hon. member for Bonaventure put forth in support of his stand, was drawn from three privy council decisions and from the constitution; he mentioned sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. Obviously, when one refers to legislation which at first sight appears more or less clear, its text should be carefully read and considered in order to be well understood. Section 91 of the British North America Act begins with the following sentence:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
Section 92 gives a list of the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures. I quote the following excerpt:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say:
Direct taxation within the province, in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes.
I stress the following words "for provincial purposes". It is true that paragraph 3 of section 91 authorizes the Dominion Government to levy indirect taxes as well as direct taxes and I shall not argue that point. However, it seems to me that the Dominion Government is granted the power to levy direct taxes sub-

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
ject to the provisions of section 92. It is evident that those two sections should be read together. We cannot contend for one moment that the Dominion Government alone should have the power to levy direct taxes and deprive the provincial governments of the same right. It is evident that, in principle, both governments have the right to levy direct taxes.
However, there is a difference between having a right and exercising it. If my good friends will listen to me for a moment, they will see that in examining legislation such as this, it is easy to draw clear and precise conclusions but one must not confuse the issues. I repeat that it evidently follows that the Dominion Government cannot levy taxes without taking into account paragraph 2 of section 92; in other words, the provincial legislatures will first have the right to levy direct taxes needed for provincial purposes, and that necessarily follows from section 91.
Again, section 91 authorizes the Dominion Government to levy direct taxes, provided it takes into account the provisions of section 92. When a province must find revenue for provincial purposes, section 92 grants power to the provincial legislature to levy direct taxes to satisfy provincial needs. Once the province has availed itself of the right to levy taxes for provincial purposes, then and only then may the Dominion Government levy direct taxes for federal and not for provincial purposes.

May I ask the hon. member a question?
. Mr. DORION: Yes.

I want an answer
immediately. I refer to the case of Silver Brothers vs. the Attorney General of the province of Quebec and the Attorney General of Canada, which dates back to 1942, regarding bankruptcy, mentioned in the Appeal Cases, page 189. Does the hon. member not admit that in this case the judicial committee of the privy council granted to the Canadian Parliament, that is the Dominion Government, priority over the provinces in the field of direct taxation?
I have here the "Dominion Law Reports" which contain precisely the case of Silver Brothers which he quoted yesterday. I shall come to that later.
I would like an answer.
You will get it, perhaps sooner than you wish.
I gave my answer yesterday.

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if sections 91 and 92 are to be reconciled, if they have any meaning at all-for I base my contention on the law-if, as I am told, those direct taxes are to be set to rights, we must come to a logical and reasonable conclusion, based on the words I have just quoted and not on imagination. This only possible conclusion I have just expressed.
The hon. member for Bonaventure referred a moment ago to the three decisions given by the privy council which he quoted yesterday in support of his argument. Last night I took the trouble of reading those three decisions in the "Dominion Law Reports". Let us consider first the case of Forbes vs. The Attorney-General of Manitoba, which is contained in volume I of the "Dominion Law Reports" for 1937. Here is the judgment:
(Text):
The legislative authority of the provinces under section 92, (2) of the British North America Act, with respect to "direct taxation within the province," embraces the power to levy taxes upon residents of the province in respect of their incomes even though a resident be an employee or servant or officer of the dominion government, and the exercise of such power by the province is no encroachment upon the exclusive powers of the dominion parliament, to fix "the salaries and allowances of civil and other officers of the government of Canada." under section 91	(8) of the British North

Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that in an interpretation based upon the standing orders of the house, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) had no right to quote that judgment in support of his contention that the provinces have priority in the field of direct taxation.
I suggest that the judgment which the learned member has quoted and which he was kind enough to send me for perusal could not apply to such a case. Indeed, that case dealt with the Bankruptcy Act and the Special War Revenue Act, whereas the matter which was brought up concerned the two creditors of the company in bankruptcy, that is the dominion and the provincial governments. It dealt with the interpretation of a special statute and not of sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act.
Hence, the only point which I wish to make in reply to my hon. friend is that the learned judges of the privy council have clearly stated, in the judgment which has been quoted, that they did not intend to give priority to the
provincial government. Let me read the decision reported on page 676 of the "Dominion Law Reports" for 1932:
(Text):
Now, looking at s. .17 and the way it speaks of the preference, it would not be difficult to hold that it was a rule only applicable in bankruptcy. If that is so, then the matter is ended for bankruptcy is head 21 of s. 91. But let it be assumed that it is rather a natural concomitant of taxation, then the case falls clearly under the fourth head laid down by Lord Tomlin. It runs thus:
"There can be a domain in which provincial and dominion legislation may overlap in which case neither legislation will be ultra vires if the field is clear, but if the field is not clear and the two legislations meet the dominion legislation must prevail."
As a matter of fact, this is the textual reproduction of what has been said by Lord Dunedin as long ago as '1907, in the case of G.T.R. v. A.G. Can., (1907) A.C. 65. Now, here so far as taxation itself is concerned, the field is clear. The two taxations, dominion and provincial, can stand side by side without interfering with each other, but as soon as you come to the concomitant privileges of absolute priority they cannot stand side by side and must clash; consequently the dominion must prevail.
(Translation):
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in view of this quotation I may conclude that the hon. member, though he be independent, should not have been so independent of the written word as to infer that section 92 should apply without any reference to section 91 of the British North America Act.
